topics.title: What makes something living, and how diverse is life?

learn.hook: A crystal of salt grows in brine and a mule cannot reproduce. So which of them is alive? Biology starts by answering exactly this.
points: Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response to surroundings (consciousness). Metabolism and cellular organisation are the defining features.
Growth alone cannot define life: non-living mountains, sand mounds and crystals also grow, by accumulation of material on the outer surface. Living organisms grow from inside.
Reproduction alone cannot define life: mules, sterile worker bees and infertile couples do not reproduce, yet they are alive.
Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in the body. No non-living object shows metabolism, so it is a defining property of life.
Biodiversity means the number and variety of organisms on Earth. About 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described so far, and many more are still unknown.

example.q: Explain why a sterile worker honeybee is classed as living even though it never reproduces.
steps: Reproduction is not shown by every living individual, so it cannot be a defining feature.
The worker bee shows metabolism: it digests nectar, respires and builds wax.
It also shows cellular organisation and responds to stimuli such as light and smell.
Metabolism and cellular organisation are defining features of life.
example.answer: It is living because it has cellular organisation and metabolism; reproduction is not a defining property.

learn.reallife: India is one of the world's 17 megadiverse countries. The Western Ghats and the north-east alone hold thousands of plant and animal species, many found nowhere else.

games.title: Living or not? Test the claims
items: Growth is a defining property of living organisms.
Non-living things such as crystals and sand mounds also grow, though by external accumulation.
A mule is alive even though it cannot produce offspring.
Reproduction is not shown by every living individual, so it is not a defining feature.
Metabolism is shown by no non-living object.
Metabolism is the sum of chemical reactions in cells, so it is a defining feature of life.
About 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described so far.
This is the number of described species; the real number is much larger.
Living organisms grow by adding material only on their outer surface.
That is how non-living things grow. Organisms grow from inside by cell division and increase in mass.
Cellular organisation is a defining feature of life.
All living things are made of cells, and no non-living object is.

quiz.q: Which property is regarded as a defining feature of living organisms?
quiz.explain: No non-living object shows metabolism, so it can be used to define life. Growth and reproduction fail this test.
steps: Asked: which feature can define life, i.e. is shown by no non-living thing.
Growth is shown by crystals; reproduction is absent in mules and worker bees.
Metabolism (all chemical reactions in the body) is shown by no non-living object.
So the defining feature is Metabolism.
Answer: Metabolism
quiz.mistake: Picks the most obvious feature (growth) without checking whether non-living things show it

quiz.q: Why is growth NOT taken as a defining property of living things?
quiz.explain: Crystals and sand mounds increase in size by accumulation of material on the surface, so growth is not unique to life.
steps: Asked: why growth fails as a defining feature of life.
Mountains, sand mounds and crystals also grow, by adding material on the outer surface.
A feature shared with non-living things cannot define life.
So: non-living objects such as crystals and mountains also grow.
Answer: Non-living objects such as crystals and mountains also grow
quiz.mistake: Forgets that non-living things can also increase in size
options: Non-living objects such as crystals and mountains also grow
Living organisms never grow after birth

quiz.q: A worker bee, a mule and an infertile human have one thing in common. What is it?
quiz.explain: All three are alive but cannot produce offspring, which shows reproduction is not a defining feature of life.
steps: List what each lacks: a worker bee, a mule and an infertile human all cannot produce offspring.
Yet all three metabolise, are made of cells and respond to stimuli, so they are alive.
Common feature: they are living but do not reproduce.
Answer: They are living but do not reproduce
quiz.mistake: Assumes anything that cannot reproduce must be non-living
options: They are living but do not reproduce
They are not made of cells

quiz.q: How does growth in living organisms differ from growth in a salt crystal?
quiz.explain: Living organisms grow by cell division and increase in mass from within, while non-living things grow by external accumulation.
steps: Living organisms grow from inside, by cell division and increase in mass.
A salt crystal grows only by accumulation of material on its outer surface.
So: organisms grow from inside; the crystal grows by adding material on its outer surface.
The reversed statement (organisms on the surface, crystal from inside) is wrong.
Answer: Organisms grow from inside; the crystal grows by adding material on its outer surface
quiz.mistake: Thinks all growth is the same process
options: Organisms grow only on the surface; the crystal grows from inside
Organisms grow from inside; the crystal grows by adding material on its outer surface
Both grow in exactly the same way

quiz.q: About how many species have been described so far on Earth?
quiz.explain: Taxonomists have named and described roughly 1.7 to 1.8 million species; many more remain undiscovered.
steps: Recall the figure from the lesson: about 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described.
Check the unit: million, not thousand or hundreds of millions.
Answer: 1.7 to 1.8 million
quiz.mistake: Slips by a factor of a thousand or ten when recalling the figure

quiz.q: The term biodiversity refers to:
quiz.explain: Biodiversity is the variety and number of living organisms in an area or on Earth as a whole.
steps: Biodiversity = the number and variety (types) of organisms on Earth.
It covers all organisms, not only plants, and is not about fossils or mass.
Answer: The number and types of organisms present on Earth
quiz.mistake: Restricts biodiversity to one group of organisms
options: Only the number of plant species
The number and types of organisms present on Earth
The total mass of all animals

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Reproduction cannot be an all-inclusive defining feature of living organisms. Reason (R): Many living organisms, such as mules and sterile worker bees, do not reproduce.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and the existence of living but non-reproducing organisms is exactly why reproduction cannot define life.
steps: A: reproduction cannot define all living things. True.
R: mules and sterile worker bees are alive but do not reproduce. True.
R gives the exact reason A holds, so both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to see the reason directly explains the assertion

quiz.q: A student says, 'A candle flame grows, uses oxygen and gives out CO₂, so it is alive.' What is the best reply?
quiz.explain: Life is defined by cellular organisation and metabolism inside cells. A flame shows neither, even if it looks like it grows and 'breathes'.
steps: Test the flame against the defining features: cellular organisation and metabolism.
A flame has no cells and no metabolism; its 'growth' and gas use are not defining features.
So the flame is not alive; the student is wrong.
Answer: A flame has no cells and no metabolism; the features it shows are not defining features of life
quiz.mistake: Confuses look-alike features with the defining features of life
options: A flame is alive because it grows
A flame has no cells and no metabolism; the features it shows are not defining features of life
Flames are alive only while burning
The student is right because it uses oxygen

teach.ask: Gappu holds up a growing sugar crystal: 'It grows, so it is alive, right? Tell me what really makes something living!'
teach.praise: Tweet! So growth fools us, but metabolism and cells never lie. Got it!
teach.nudge: Hmm, crystals grow too. What feature do only living things have?

revise.summary: Living things show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response, but only metabolism and cellular organisation define life. Biodiversity is the number and variety of organisms; about 1.7–1.8 million species are described.
focus: Why growth and reproduction are not defining features of life
Metabolism and cellular organisation as the defining features
Difference between growth from inside and growth by surface accumulation
Meaning of biodiversity and the number of described species
remember: Defining features of life: metabolism and cellular organisation
Metabolism = sum of all chemical reactions in the body
Described species: about 1.7 to 1.8 million
traps: Don't call growth a defining feature: crystals and mountains also grow
Don't say non-reproducing organisms (mule, worker bee) are non-living

topics.title: Why scientific names? Identification and nomenclature

learn.hook: Brinjal, baingan, vankaya, kathirikai, aubergine, eggplant: six names for one vegetable. A scientist in Chennai and one in Berlin need one name they both trust.
points: Local names of the same organism differ from place to place, even within one country, so a standard name is needed worldwide.
Identification: describing an organism correctly so that we know exactly which organism it is. It comes before naming.
Nomenclature: giving a correct scientific name to an organism that has been identified.
Scientific names follow international codes: ICBN (International Code for Botanical Nomenclature) for plants and ICZN (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature) for animals.
These codes make sure each organism has only one correct name, and that no name is used for two different organisms.

example.q: Put the steps in order: a new plant found in Meghalaya must be given a scientific name.
steps: First describe its features accurately (identification).
Check it against known plants to confirm it is new.
Name it following the rules of ICBN (nomenclature).
example.answer: Identification first, then nomenclature under ICBN.

learn.reallife: When AIIMS doctors report a fungal infection, or the Botanical Survey of India lists a new orchid from Arunachal Pradesh, they use scientific names so labs anywhere can understand them.

games.title: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Giving it a correct scientific name

items.text: Naming an organism is possible only after it is correctly ___.
Animal names are governed by the ___.
Plant names are governed by the ___.
Common names are not useful in science because they ___ from place to place.

quiz.q: Why do biologists need scientific names instead of local names?
quiz.explain: The same organism has many local names, and the same local name may refer to different organisms. A standard name avoids confusion.
steps: The same organism has different local names in different places.
The same local name may even refer to different organisms, causing confusion.
So a standard scientific name is needed: local names differ from place to place and cause confusion.
Answer: Local names differ from place to place and cause confusion
quiz.mistake: Thinks the issue is length or pronunciation rather than confusion
options: Local names are always too long
Local names differ from place to place and cause confusion
Scientific names are easier to pronounce

quiz.q: Which process must come first before an organism can be named?
quiz.explain: You can only name an organism once you have described it correctly and know what it is.
steps: Identification = describing an organism correctly so we know exactly what it is.
Nomenclature (naming) can only follow once the organism is identified.
So identification must come first.
Answer: Identification
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of identification and nomenclature

quiz.q: ICZN provides rules for naming:
quiz.explain: ICZN is the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature, used for animals.
steps: ICZN = International Code of Zoological Nomenclature.
'Zoological' refers to animals.
So ICZN gives rules for naming animals (ICBN is for plants).
Answer: Animals
quiz.mistake: Confuses ICZN with ICBN

quiz.q: The full form of ICBN is:
quiz.explain: ICBN stands for International Code for Botanical Nomenclature, which governs plant names.
steps: ICBN governs names of plants.
B stands for Botanical, N for Nomenclature.
Full form: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature.
Answer: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature
quiz.mistake: Guesses a full form from the letters without knowing it

quiz.q: Nomenclature means:
quiz.explain: Nomenclature is naming. Grouping is classification and relationships are part of systematics.
steps: Nomenclature means naming.
It is giving a correct scientific name to an organism already identified.
Grouping is classification, not nomenclature.
Answer: Giving a correct scientific name to an organism
quiz.mistake: Confuses nomenclature with classification
options: Giving a correct scientific name to an organism
Describing the habitat of an organism

quiz.q: A biologist correctly describes the features of a new beetle so that it can be told apart from all others. This step is:
quiz.explain: Correct description of an organism is identification; naming comes after it.
steps: The biologist describes the beetle's features so it can be told apart from others.
Correct description of an organism is identification.
Naming (nomenclature) comes only after this, so the step is identification.
Answer: Identification
quiz.mistake: Thinks describing and naming are the same step

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Each organism can have only one correct scientific name. Reason (R): International codes such as ICBN and ICZN make sure a given name is used for only one organism.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and the codes are the reason a scientific name is unique and universal.
steps: A: each organism has only one correct scientific name. True.
R: ICBN and ICZN ensure a name is used for one organism only. True.
The codes are why names are unique, so both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the uniqueness of names to the codes

quiz.q: Which statement about common names is correct?
quiz.explain: Common names depend on local language and region, which is exactly why scientific names are needed.
steps: Common names depend on local language and region.
So one organism can have different common names in different regions.
They are not uniform, not in Latin and not governed by ICBN.
Answer: The same organism may have different common names in different regions
quiz.mistake: Assumes common names are standardised
options: Common names are the same in every language
The same organism may have different common names in different regions
Common names are always in Latin
Common names are governed by ICBN

teach.ask: Gappu calls the same bird 'kauwa' in Delhi and 'kaka' in Kerala. 'Why can't scientists just use local names?' Explain!
teach.praise: Chirp! One name, one organism, decided by the codes. Neat!
teach.nudge: Good, but who makes the naming rules for plants and animals?

revise.summary: Local names of an organism differ from place to place, so biologists identify an organism first and then give it one standard scientific name under international codes: ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals.

Identification versus nomenclature, and their order
Full forms and scope of ICBN and ICZN
remember: Identification = correct description of an organism; it comes first
Nomenclature = giving a correct scientific name
ICBN: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (plants); ICZN: International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (animals)
traps: Don't mix up ICBN (plants) and ICZN (animals)

topics.title: Binomial nomenclature: writing scientific names right

learn.hook: A board examiner can cut marks for writing 'Mangifera Indica'. One wrong capital letter, and the name is wrong. Let's get it right forever.
points: Binomial nomenclature was proposed by Carolus Linnaeus. Every scientific name has two parts: the generic name (genus) and the specific epithet (species).
Names are in Latin or are latinised, whatever their origin.
When printed, the name is in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately to show their Latin origin.
The genus name begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter. Example: Mangifera indica.
The name of the author who first described the species appears after the epithet in abbreviated form, e.g. Mangifera indica Linn. (Linn. = Linnaeus).

example.q: A student writes the human scientific name as 'Homo Sapiens' in her answer sheet with no underline. Correct it.
steps: Genus Homo starts with a capital: correct.
Specific epithet must start with a small letter: sapiens.
Handwritten names must be underlined, each word separately.
example.answer: Homo sapiens, with 'Homo' and 'sapiens' each underlined separately.

learn.reallife: The mango, India's national fruit, is Mangifera indica, and the peacock, the national bird, is Pavo cristatus. 'indica' itself honours India.

games.title: Spot the correct rule
items: The specific epithet starts with a capital letter.
Only the genus name starts with a capital letter.
Handwritten scientific names are underlined separately.
Each word is underlined on its own to show Latin origin.
Binomial nomenclature was proposed by Carolus Linnaeus.
Linnaeus introduced the two-part naming system.
Printed scientific names appear in bold capitals.
In Mangifera indica Linn., 'Linn.' is the name of the genus.
'Linn.' is the abbreviated author name, Linnaeus.
The first word of a binomial is the generic name.
Generic name first, specific epithet second.

quiz.q: Who proposed binomial nomenclature?
quiz.explain: Carolus Linnaeus introduced the two-word naming system used for all organisms.
steps: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-part name.
This system was proposed by Carolus Linnaeus.
Answer: Carolus Linnaeus
quiz.mistake: Confuses the founder of naming with the founder of the five-kingdom system

quiz.q: A magazine prints the lion's name as 'Panthera Leo'. Which rule does this break?
quiz.explain: Genus takes a capital letter and the epithet a small letter, so it should be Panthera leo (in italics in print).
steps: Rule: genus starts with a capital letter, specific epithet with a small letter.
'Panthera Leo' has a capital L in the epithet.
Correct form is Panthera leo, so the broken rule is: epithet must begin with a small letter.
Answer: The specific epithet must begin with a small letter
quiz.mistake: Capitalises the specific epithet as in an English proper noun
options: The specific epithet must begin with a small letter
The name must be underlined in print
The genus must begin with a small letter
The author's name must always be written

quiz.q: In Mangifera indica Linn., the word 'indica' is the:
quiz.explain: The second word of a binomial is the specific epithet.
steps: A binomial has two parts: genus (first word) and specific epithet (second word).
In Mangifera indica Linn., 'indica' is the second word.
So 'indica' is the specific epithet.
Answer: Specific epithet
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of the two parts

quiz.q: In Mangifera indica Linn., what does 'Linn.' tell us?
quiz.explain: The abbreviated author name follows the epithet; here it stands for Linnaeus.
steps: The author's name comes after the epithet in abbreviated form.
'Linn.' stands for Linnaeus, who first described the species.
So it tells us the scientist who first described the species.
Answer: The scientist who first described the species
quiz.mistake: Thinks the third word is part of the classification
options: The scientist who first described the species

quiz.q: How should a scientific name be written in a handwritten answer?
quiz.explain: Handwritten names are underlined, each word separately, to show their Latin origin.
steps: Printed names are in italics; handwritten names are underlined.
Each of the two words is underlined separately to show Latin origin.
Answer: Each of the two words underlined separately
quiz.mistake: Uses a single continuous underline
options: With one line under both words together
Each of the two words underlined separately

quiz.q: Scientific names are taken from which language, or are made to fit it?
quiz.explain: Biological names are Latin or latinised, whatever their source.
steps: Scientific names are in Latin or are latinised, whatever their origin.
Answer: Latin
quiz.mistake: Thinks scientific names come from the discoverer's language

quiz.q: A textbook prints 'Solanum tuberosum' in italics. What does 'Solanum' denote?
quiz.explain: The first word, beginning with a capital letter, is the genus.
steps: In a binomial, the first word, starting with a capital letter, is the genus.
'Solanum' is the first word of Solanum tuberosum.
So Solanum denotes the genus.
Answer: The genus
quiz.mistake: Thinks the first word is the species

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The specific epithet in a binomial name begins with a small letter. Reason (R): The generic name always ends in '-ae'.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The assertion is a correct rule. The reason is false: generic names such as Homo or Panthera do not end in '-ae'; the ending '-ae' is typical of plant family names.
steps: A: the specific epithet begins with a small letter. True rule.
R: generic names always end in '-ae'. False: Homo and Panthera do not.
So A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Accepts a made-up rule because it sounds technical

teach.ask: Gappu wrote 'Mangifera Indica' on his test and lost marks. Explain the rules of writing a scientific name!
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Capital genus, small epithet, italics or underline. Full marks next time!
teach.nudge: Almost! What about capital and small letters, and how is it shown in print or handwriting?

revise.summary: Linnaeus's binomial nomenclature gives every organism a two-part Latin name: genus (capital letter) and specific epithet (small letter), italicised in print or underlined separately by hand, with the author's name abbreviated after it.
focus: The two parts of a scientific name and how to identify each
Rules for capitals, italics and underlining
Meaning of the author abbreviation such as Linn.
remember: Proposed by Carolus Linnaeus
Genus: capital first letter; specific epithet: small first letter
Printed in italics; handwritten with each word underlined separately
Example: Mangifera indica Linn.
traps: Don't capitalise the specific epithet (Panthera leo, not Panthera Leo)
Don't draw one line under both words when handwriting; underline each separately

learn.hook: Supermarkets put all dals in one aisle and all spices in another so you find things fast. Biologists do the same with 1.7 million species.
points: Classification: grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters.
Taxon: a group at any level of classification. 'Plants', 'animals', 'mammals' and 'dogs' are all taxa.
Taxonomy includes characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature of organisms.
Bases of modern taxonomic studies: external and internal structure, cell structure, development process and ecological information.
Systematics (from Latin 'systema', systematic arrangement) studies the kinds and diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships. It is broader than taxonomy.

steps: A taxon is any group at any level of classification.
Mammals form a group at class level, so they are a taxon.
Wheat refers to a group at species level, which is also a taxon.
example.answer: Yes, both are taxa; one at class level, the other at species level.

learn.reallife: Seed banks of the ICAR and the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi store lakhs of crop samples. Without careful classification, finding the right rice variety would be impossible.

games.title: Is it a basis of modern taxonomic study?

quiz.q: A group of organisms at any level of classification is called a:
quiz.explain: Taxon is the general word for a group at any rank, from kingdom down to species.
steps: A taxon is a group at any level (rank) of classification.
It applies from kingdom down to species, not to one rank only.
Answer: Taxon
quiz.mistake: Thinks taxon means only one particular rank

quiz.q: Which word comes from the Latin 'systema'?
quiz.explain: Systematics comes from 'systema', meaning systematic arrangement of organisms.
steps: 'Systema' is Latin for systematic arrangement.
Systematics takes its name from this word.
Answer: Systematics
quiz.mistake: Links taxonomy to the Latin root

quiz.q: Systematics differs from taxonomy because it also includes:
quiz.explain: Systematics covers identification, nomenclature and classification and also takes account of evolutionary relationships.
steps: Taxonomy: characterisation, identification, classification, nomenclature.
Systematics also takes account of evolutionary relationships between organisms.
So the extra part is evolutionary relationships.
Answer: Evolutionary relationships between organisms
quiz.mistake: Treats taxonomy and systematics as identical

quiz.q: Which set lists the processes included in taxonomy?
quiz.explain: Taxonomy brings together characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature.
steps: Taxonomy includes four processes in the lesson.
They are characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature.
The other sets are life processes or evolution steps, not taxonomy.
Answer: Characterisation, identification, classification, nomenclature
quiz.mistake: Mixes up taxonomy with physiology or evolution

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a basis of modern taxonomic studies?
quiz.explain: Taxonomy uses structure, cells, development and ecology. Market price has nothing to do with relationships.
steps: Bases of modern taxonomy: external and internal structure, cell structure, development, ecology.
Commercial price says nothing about an organism's features or relationships.
So the commercial price is NOT a basis.
Answer: The commercial price of the organism
quiz.mistake: Picks a real character because it sounds unfamiliar
options: The commercial price of the organism

quiz.q: Grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters is:
quiz.explain: This is the definition of classification.
steps: Grouping organisms into convenient categories on easily observable characters is the definition of classification.
Naming is nomenclature; describing is identification.
Answer: Classification
quiz.mistake: Confuses classification with identification

quiz.q: 'Dogs', 'mammals' and 'plants' are examples of:
quiz.explain: Each is a group at some level of classification, so each is a taxon.
steps: A taxon is a group at any level of classification.
Dogs, mammals and plants are groups at different levels.
So they are taxa at different levels.
Answer: Taxa at different levels
quiz.mistake: Thinks only a species can be a taxon
options: Common names with no scientific meaning

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Taxonomy is a broader study than systematics. Reason (R): Systematics also considers the evolutionary relationships between organisms.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: systematics is the broader study, not taxonomy. R is true: systematics adds evolutionary relationships to identification, naming and classification, which is exactly why it is broader.
steps: A says taxonomy is broader than systematics. False: systematics is broader.
R says systematics also considers evolutionary relationships. True.
So A is false, R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Judges the assertion true just because the reason is a correct fact

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Taxon, taxonomy, systematics... aren't they all the same word?' Untangle them for him!
teach.praise: Chirp! A taxon is a group, taxonomy names and sorts, systematics adds family history. Clear!
teach.nudge: Nice! But what extra thing does systematics look at?

revise.summary: Classification groups organisms by observable characters; any group at any rank is a taxon. Taxonomy covers characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature, while systematics also studies evolutionary relationships.
focus: Definitions of classification, taxon, taxonomy and systematics
Why systematics is broader than taxonomy
Bases of modern taxonomic studies
remember: Taxon = a group at any level of classification
Taxonomy = characterisation + identification + classification + nomenclature
Systematics (Latin 'systema') adds evolutionary relationships
traps: Don't say taxonomy is broader than systematics; it is the other way round
Don't think a taxon means only a species; it can be any rank

learn.hook: Your address goes Country → State → City → Street → House. Each organism has a 'biological address' too, and species is the house number.
points: Taxonomic hierarchy: categories arranged in a step-like order, kingdom at the top and species at the bottom.
Each category (rank) is a unit of classification and represents a taxon at that level.
Species: a group of individuals with fundamental similarities. It is the basic unit of classification. Examples: leo (lion), tigris (tiger), pardus (leopard) in Panthera.
Genus: a group of related species with more characters in common than species of other genera. Panthera has lion, tiger and leopard; Solanum has potato (S. tuberosum) and brinjal (S. melongena).
Lion, tiger and leopard share many features, so they are placed in one genus, Panthera; the cat is in a different genus, Felis.

example.q: Why are potato and brinjal in the same genus but given different species names?
steps: Both share many fundamental features, so they belong to the genus Solanum.
They differ in key characters, so each is a separate species.
Hence potato is Solanum tuberosum and brinjal is Solanum melongena.
example.answer: Same genus Solanum, different species: tuberosum and melongena.

learn.reallife: The Bengal tiger in Sundarbans, the Asiatic lion in Gir and the leopards of Mumbai's Sanjay Gandhi National Park are all members of one genus: Panthera.

Lion, tiger and leopard all belong to the genus ___.
A group of related species forms a ___.

games.title: Species epithet to animal or plant

quiz.q: Which is the basic unit of classification?
quiz.explain: Species is the lowest category and the basic unit; all higher categories are built from species.
steps: The hierarchy runs from kingdom (top) to species (bottom).
Species is the lowest category and all higher ranks are built from species.
So the basic unit is species.
Answer: Species
quiz.mistake: Thinks the highest category is the basic one

quiz.q: Lion, tiger and leopard are placed in the same:
quiz.explain: All three belong to the genus Panthera but are different species.
steps: Lion (leo), tiger (tigris) and leopard (pardus) share many features.
They are placed in one genus, Panthera, as different species.
Answer: Genus
quiz.mistake: Thinks similar animals must be the same species

quiz.q: Solanum tuberosum and Solanum melongena belong to the same genus. What does this tell us?
quiz.explain: A genus groups related species with many shared characters.
steps: Same genus name (Solanum) means the two are related species in one genus.
A genus groups species with more characters in common than with species of other genera.
Different epithets show they are not the same species.
Answer: They share more characters with each other than with species of other genera
quiz.mistake: Thinks same genus means same species
options: They share more characters with each other than with species of other genera

quiz.q: Arranging taxonomic categories in a step-like order from kingdom to species is called:
quiz.explain: The ordered sequence of ranks is the taxonomic hierarchy.
steps: Categories arranged step-like from kingdom down to species form a hierarchy.
This is called the taxonomic hierarchy.
Answer: Taxonomic hierarchy
quiz.mistake: Confuses hierarchy with naming

quiz.q: A taxonomic category, such as 'family', is best described as:
quiz.explain: Each category is a rank in the hierarchy and a unit of classification, and the group placed at that rank is a taxon.
steps: Each category in the hierarchy is a rank.
Each rank is a unit of classification, and the group at that rank is a taxon.
So family is a rank that represents a unit of classification.
Answer: A rank that represents a unit of classification
quiz.mistake: Thinks a category refers to one individual
options: A rank that represents a unit of classification

quiz.q: Which genus includes the potato?
quiz.explain: Potato is Solanum tuberosum.
steps: Potato is Solanum tuberosum.
The first word is the genus.
So potato is in genus Solanum.
Answer: Solanum
quiz.mistake: Confuses plant genera with animal genera

quiz.q: A 'species' is best defined as:
quiz.explain: Species is a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities.
steps: Species = a group of individuals with fundamental similarities.
Answer: A group of individuals with fundamental similarities
quiz.mistake: Confuses species with family
options: A group of unrelated organisms in one area
A group of individuals with fundamental similarities

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Species is considered the basic unit of classification. Reason (R): All higher categories such as genus and family are formed by grouping species on shared characters.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true and the reason explains why species is basic: everything above is built from species.
steps: A: species is the basic unit of classification. True.
R: higher categories are formed by grouping species on shared characters. True.
R explains why species is basic, so both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Misses that higher ranks are made by grouping species

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Lions and tigers look different, so why do they share a genus?' Teach him about species and genus!
teach.praise: Tweet! Different species, same genus, because they share lots of features. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good! But what is the link between a species and a genus?

revise.summary: The taxonomic hierarchy arranges ranks from kingdom down to species. Species, a group of individuals with fundamental similarities, is the basic unit; a genus groups related species, e.g. Panthera (lion, tiger, leopard) and Solanum (potato, brinjal).
focus: Meaning of taxonomic hierarchy and category (rank)
Species as the basic unit of classification
Examples of genus: Panthera and Solanum
remember: Species = group of individuals with fundamental similarities
Genus = group of related species
Panthera leo, P. tigris, P. pardus; Solanum tuberosum (potato), S. melongena (brinjal)
traps: Don't say lion, tiger and leopard are the same species; they share only the genus
Don't place the cat in Panthera; it is in genus Felis

topics.title: Family, order, class, phylum and kingdom

learn.hook: Going up the hierarchy is like zooming out on Google Maps: you see more and more places, but each one shows fewer shared details.
points: Family: a group of related genera. Felidae (Panthera, Felis), Canidae (dogs) and Solanaceae (Solanum, Petunia, Datura) are families.
Order: an assemblage of families with a few similar characters. Carnivora includes Felidae and Canidae; Polymoniales includes Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae.
Class: related orders. Mammalia includes orders such as Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and Carnivora (tiger, cat, dog). Dicotyledonae is a plant class.
Phylum (animals) or Division (plants): related classes. Chordata includes Mammalia, Aves, Reptilia and Amphibia. Kingdom is the highest category (Animalia, Plantae).
As we go up from species to kingdom, the number of common characters decreases, and the number of organisms in the group increases.

example.q: Arrange in ascending order (lowest first): Order, Species, Kingdom, Family, Class, Genus, Phylum.
steps: Ascending means from the lowest rank to the highest.
Lowest rank is species, then genus, family, order, class, phylum, and kingdom on top.
example.answer: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom

learn.reallife: Indian Railways groups its trains into zones, divisions and routes. Bigger units hold more trains but those trains share fewer specific features, just like higher taxa.

quiz.q: Felidae and Canidae are placed in the same:
quiz.explain: Cat family (Felidae) and dog family (Canidae) are both in the order Carnivora.
steps: Felidae is the cat family; Canidae is the dog family.
Both families are placed in the order Carnivora.
Answer: Order Carnivora
quiz.mistake: Assumes both families must be in one family

quiz.q: Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae are families placed in the order:
quiz.explain: Polymoniales includes Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae, based on floral characters.
steps: An order is an assemblage of families with a few similar characters.
Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae are both in the order Polymoniales.
Answer: Polymoniales
quiz.mistake: Mixes plant and animal orders

quiz.q: In plants, the category equivalent to 'phylum' in animals is:
quiz.explain: Plants use the term Division in place of Phylum.
steps: Animals use the rank phylum for a group of related classes.
Plants use Division in its place.
Answer: Division
quiz.mistake: Thinks plants use 'phylum' too or picks the next rank down

quiz.q: As we move from species to kingdom, the number of common characters among members:
quiz.explain: Higher categories are broader groups, so the members share fewer characters.
steps: Going up from species to kingdom, each group becomes broader.
Broader groups contain more organisms with fewer shared characters.
So common characters decrease.
Answer: Decreases
quiz.mistake: Thinks a bigger group means more shared features

quiz.q: Which is the highest taxonomic category?
quiz.explain: Kingdom is at the top of the hierarchy.
steps: The hierarchy runs species → genus → family → order → class → phylum → kingdom.
Kingdom is at the top.
Answer: Kingdom
quiz.mistake: Confuses top and bottom of the hierarchy

quiz.q: Monkeys, gorillas and gibbons are placed in order Primata, which belongs to class:
quiz.explain: Primata and Carnivora are orders within the class Mammalia.
steps: Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) is an order.
Primata and Carnivora are orders within the class Mammalia.
Answer: Mammalia
quiz.mistake: Does not link orders with their class

quiz.q: How many obligate (main) categories are there from kingdom to species?
quiz.explain: Kingdom, phylum/division, class, order, family, genus and species: seven categories.
steps: List the categories: kingdom, phylum/division, class, order, family, genus, species.
Count them: 7.
Answer: 7
quiz.mistake: Forgets phylum or genus while counting

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A family usually contains more organisms than a genus does. Reason (R): Members of a family share more characters than members of a genus.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A family is a group of genera, so it contains more organisms. But members of a family share fewer characters, not more, so R is false.
steps: A: a family contains more organisms than a genus. True, as a family is a group of genera.
R: family members share more characters than genus members. False: they share fewer.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Mixes up group size with number of shared characters

teach.ask: Gappu climbs a 'taxonomy ladder' and asks: 'Why do the groups get bigger but less alike as I go up?' Explain!
teach.praise: Chirp! Higher ranks hold more organisms that share fewer characters. Wonderful!
teach.nudge: Good start! What happens to the number of shared characters as you go up?

revise.summary: Related genera form a family, families an order, orders a class, classes a phylum (division in plants), and phyla a kingdom. Going up, groups hold more organisms but share fewer characters.
focus: Correct order of the seven obligate categories
Examples: Felidae, Canidae in Carnivora; Solanaceae, Convolvulaceae in Polymoniales
How the number of common characters changes up the hierarchy
remember: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom
Division in plants = phylum in animals
Up the hierarchy: common characters decrease, number of organisms increases
traps: Don't say higher categories share more characters; they share fewer
Don't call Primata a family or class; it is an order in class Mammalia

topics.title: Classifying common organisms: man, housefly, mango, wheat

learn.hook: Your breakfast roti (wheat) and the fly hovering over it have full biological addresses. Can you read them?
points: Man: Homo sapiens; family Hominidae; order Primata; class Mammalia; phylum Chordata; kingdom Animalia.
Housefly: Musca domestica; family Muscidae; order Diptera; class Insecta; phylum Arthropoda; kingdom Animalia.
Mango: Mangifera indica; family Anacardiaceae; order Sapindales; class Dicotyledonae; division Angiospermae; kingdom Plantae.
Wheat: Triticum aestivum; family Poaceae; order Poales; class Monocotyledonae; division Angiospermae; kingdom Plantae.
Mango and wheat share the division Angiospermae but differ from class downwards: mango is a dicot, wheat a monocot.

example.q: At which level do mango and wheat stop sharing the same category?
steps: Kingdom: both Plantae.
Division: both Angiospermae.
Class: mango is Dicotyledonae, wheat is Monocotyledonae.
example.answer: They separate at the class level.

learn.reallife: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) from Punjab and Madhya Pradesh fills the FCI granaries, and Alphonso mangoes (Mangifera indica) from Ratnagiri are exported worldwide.

quiz.q: The housefly belongs to the order:
quiz.explain: Musca domestica is placed in family Muscidae, order Diptera, class Insecta.
steps: Housefly: Musca domestica, family Muscidae.
Its order is Diptera, class Insecta.
Answer: Diptera
quiz.mistake: Matches the wrong order to the organism

quiz.q: The family of mango is:
quiz.explain: Mangifera indica belongs to the family Anacardiaceae.
steps: Mango: Mangifera indica.
Its family is Anacardiaceae, order Sapindales.
Answer: Anacardiaceae
quiz.mistake: Picks the wheat family by mistake

quiz.q: Wheat belongs to class:
quiz.explain: Wheat is a monocot: class Monocotyledonae, order Poales, family Poaceae.
steps: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a monocot.
Class Monocotyledonae, order Poales, family Poaceae.
Answer: Monocotyledonae
quiz.mistake: Assumes all angiosperm crops are dicots

quiz.q: Human beings belong to the family:
quiz.explain: Homo sapiens is in family Hominidae; Primata is the order, not the family.
steps: Man: Homo sapiens, family Hominidae, order Primata.
Primata is the order, not the family.
Answer: Hominidae
quiz.mistake: Confuses order Primata with the family

quiz.q: Which category is shared by man and housefly?
quiz.explain: Man is a chordate and the housefly an arthropod, so they share only the kingdom.
steps: Man: phylum Chordata, class Mammalia. Housefly: phylum Arthropoda, class Insecta.
They differ from phylum downwards.
So they share only Kingdom Animalia.
Answer: Kingdom Animalia
quiz.mistake: Assumes all animals share the phylum

quiz.q: Which is the correct classification of mango?
quiz.explain: Mango: division Angiospermae, class Dicotyledonae, order Sapindales, family Anacardiaceae.
steps: Mango: Plantae → Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera.
Monocotyledonae and Poales belong to wheat, not mango.
Answer: Plantae → Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera
quiz.mistake: Mixes the mango and wheat ranks
options: Animalia → Chordata → Mammalia → Primata → Hominidae → Mangifera
Plantae → Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera
Plantae → Angiospermae → Monocotyledonae → Poales → Poaceae → Mangifera
Plantae → Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Poales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera

quiz.q: The housefly's phylum is:
quiz.explain: Insects such as the housefly have jointed legs and belong to phylum Arthropoda.
steps: Housefly is an insect with jointed legs.
Insects belong to phylum Arthropoda.
Answer: Arthropoda
quiz.mistake: Thinks every animal is a chordate

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mango and wheat are placed in the same division. Reason (R): Both are flowering plants with seeds enclosed in fruits.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both belong to division Angiospermae, the flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed in fruits, so R explains A.
steps: A: mango and wheat are in the same division, Angiospermae. True.
R: both are flowering plants with seeds enclosed in fruits. True.
That is the feature of Angiospermae, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect angiosperm features to the shared division

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know where his roti comes from 'biologically'. Give him wheat's full classification!
teach.praise: Tweet! Triticum aestivum, a monocot angiosperm. My roti has a family tree!
teach.nudge: Nice! Which class, monocot or dicot, and which family?

revise.summary: Man, housefly, mango and wheat show how the hierarchy is used: man and housefly share only kingdom Animalia, while mango (dicot) and wheat (monocot) share kingdom Plantae and division Angiospermae and separate at class.
focus: Full classification of man, housefly, mango and wheat
Finding the level at which two organisms stop sharing a category
Distinguishing order from family names (Primata vs Hominidae)
remember: Man: Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata
Housefly: Muscidae, Diptera, Insecta, Arthropoda
Mango: Anacardiaceae, Sapindales, Dicotyledonae, Angiospermae
Wheat: Poaceae, Poales, Monocotyledonae, Angiospermae
traps: Don't call Primata the family of man; the family is Hominidae
Don't put mango in Poales or wheat in Dicotyledonae
